chapters.title: 1. What a rocket is, in one page
paragraphs: A rocket is a tank of propellant with an engine at the bottom and a reason to go at the top. Everything else is there to keep those three alive.

The engine throws exhaust out the back as fast as it can. The rocket moves forward because of that push: Newton's third law. The faster the exhaust (that is what Isp measures), the less propellant you need for the same trip.

Almost all of the mass on the stand is propellant. A ship that is 85 % fuel by mass is normal. That is why every kilogram of hardware or samples matters: you pay for it with fuel, and fuel with more fuel.

Order of a sensible stack, top to bottom: nose cone, capsule (with the crew), heat shield, tanks, engine. Side-mounted parts clamp to the tanks and the capsule; landing legs clamp to the engine so the feet reach the ground.

chapters.title: 2. Reading the numbers without fear
paragraphs: TWR (thrust-to-weight ratio): how hard the engine pushes compared with how heavy the ship is. Below 1 the ship sits on the pad. Above 1.2 it climbs briskly. Think of a car pulling a trailer uphill: more trailer, more engine.

Δv (delta-v): the total change of speed the ship can make before the tank is empty. It is your fuel budget written as speed. The trip to Mars needs a fixed amount per leg; if your Δv is bigger than the sum, you get there.

Isp (specific impulse): how efficiently the engine turns propellant into push. A higher number means each kilogram of fuel buys more Δv. Hydrogen is best but bulky; kerosene is dense and cheap; methane sits between and can be made on Mars.

Centre of mass and centre of pressure: where the ship balances, and where the air pushes on it. Keep the push behind the balance point (fins low on the stack) or the ship tries to swap ends in thick air, like an arrow thrown feathers-first.
Reliability: every part has a small chance to fail. Multiply them all and a ship with forty parts is only as good as the cheapest one. The poll warns below 80 %.

chapters.title: 3. A ship that comes back: the recipe
paragraphs: 1. Start with the capsule at the Crew Systems lab. Add a spare oxygen bottle, a radiation shelter and an antenna. No antenna means nothing you find can be sent home.

2. At Propulsion, pick an engine for the pad: a sea-level nozzle and a pump big enough that TWR stays above 1.2 with full tanks. A vacuum nozzle loses about a third of its thrust in air; it belongs on upper stages, which we do not have yet.
3. Add tanks of the same fuel as the engine until Δv covers the trip to Mars (the Telemetry board shows the legs). Tanks of a different fuel are dead weight.
4. At Structures, add a heat shield (entry heating grows with the cube of speed), landing legs, a parachute and fins low on the stack.
5. Run the static fire at the Test console. If the vehicle does not lift in the hold-down test, it will not lift on the pad either.
6. Pick a launch window at the Range terminal. The cold morning is free. Cheap seals are not rated for it: the Challenger crew learned that at 2 °C.

chapters.title: 4. Lessons people paid for
paragraphs: Challenger, 1986: an O-ring in a booster seal stiffened in the cold and let hot gas through. Engineers had warned the night before. Lesson: a warning you override is still a warning.
Columbia, 2003: a piece of foam struck the wing on ascent. The damage was small, nobody inspected it, and the heat of re-entry did the rest. Lesson: small damage kills; inspect.
Apollo 13, 1970: a tank exploded on the way to the Moon. Calm problem-solving brought everyone home. Lesson: a shelter, a plan and a cool head are hardware too.
Mars Climate Orbiter, 1999: one team used pounds-force, the other newtons. The probe burned up. Lesson: units are part of the design.

chapters.title: 5. Anatomy of a launch vehicle
paragraphs: Read a real rocket from the top down, the way the Dawn launch diagram does. Fairing: the two-piece shell that shields the payload through the air, dropped at about 100 km. Payload attach fitting: the cone that bolts the spacecraft to the stage and lets it go with springs.

Third-stage motor: a small solid motor (Dawn used a Star 48B, 66 kN for 87 seconds) spun up on a spin table so it needs no guidance; a clamp band holds it until pyrotechnic bolts cut it free. Guidance electronics: the flight computer, gyros and radios that fly the launcher, in a ring near the top of the second stage.

Second stage: a restartable liquid engine with a long vacuum bell, fed from tanks pressurised by helium spheres; nitrogen spheres feed the cold-gas thrusters that steer between burns; a miniskirt and open truss carry the loads and hold the spheres. Interstage: the hollow ring that joins the stages and hides the upper engine bell.

First stage: a fuel tank and an oxidizer tank with a stiff centerbody section between them, a wiring tunnel down the outside for cables and lines, and the main engine on a gimbal at the bottom. Thrust augmentation solids: strap-on solid motors around the base (Dawn's Delta II had nine) that give most of the push off the pad and are dropped in the first two minutes.

In this hangar every one of those pieces is a part you can choose: the design page draws your stack the same way, from nose to nozzle. Nothing separates in flight yet, so a casing or an interstage you add rides along to Mars as dry mass: that is the honest price of it until staging arrives.

chapters.title: 6. Inside the parts
paragraphs: Zoom into a part on the design page and it opens up. An engine is a turbopump (and the cycle that drives it: gas generator, staged combustion, expander, electric or none at all), an injector plate, a chamber, a nozzle skirt and an igniter. Each choice moves mass, cost, Isp or reliability, and the card says by how much.

A tank is two domes (or one shared common bulkhead), slosh baffles, insulation, pressurisation and feed lines. A capsule is a flight computer (one, three voting, or four plus a backup), a life-support loop, couches, windows and a hatch that must open outward.

Materials matter as much as shapes. Aluminium-lithium is the modern tank alloy; 2219 the cheap classic; stainless steel is heavy but happy hot and cold; carbon fibre is the lightest and the most brittle; titanium is strong, light and dear. Pressure bottles can be carbon-overwrapped, titanium or plain steel.
A rule from every accident report: the parts that failed were rarely the big ones. An O-ring, a strut, a foam block, a hatch. The small choices inside a part are where reliability is won.

chapters.title: 7. The machines in this hall
paragraphs: Any design desk (integration, propulsion, structures, crew systems, warehouse) opens the design page: the vehicle in 3D, every part labelled. Drag to turn it, scroll to zoom. Click a part to see what it is and what could replace it; zoom in on a selected part and it opens up to show what is inside.

The strip at the top shows the choices as small cards: picture, name, price. Click a card and the panel on the right tells the whole story (what it is for, pros and cons, the numbers) with an INSTALL button. The strip folds away when you want the whole screen for the vehicle.

Test console: the static fire, the hold-down liftoff test and the readiness poll. Range terminal: the launch window and its weather. This handbook: the right-hand page is yours; write what worked and what did not. It is saved with your agency.
